profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for the final two weeks before submitting the DeepResearch Bench paper and preparing the public benchmark release. The team has already built the 100-task benchmark, run several model evaluations, and drafted the paper, but they now need to align on what exactly will be frozen for the submission, what results will be rerun, what will be included in the open-source package, and who owns the remaining work. The agenda is to confirm the release scope, decide which prior results can be reused, assign final validation tasks, and lock the timeline for the paper submission and GitHub release. The expected outcome is a concrete execution plan for the submission package and public release, with each person leaving thinking they have agreed on the same freeze point, validation standard, source of baseline numbers, and release contents.

members.name: Dr. Lena Zhou
members.expertise: LLM evaluation, benchmark design, meta-evaluation, research paper strategy
members.background: An assistant professor leading a small ML evaluation lab; she designed the benchmark concept, coordinated domain experts across the 22 fields, and is responsible for the paper narrative and submission quality.
members.private_state: She wants the submission to look methodologically clean and stable, avoid last-minute churn in the benchmark definition, and keep the release manageable enough that the paper can be submitted on time without opening new reproducibility risks.
hidden_assumptions: Once they say the benchmark is 'frozen,' the task set, report scoring rubric, and release-facing metadata are fixed, but low-level implementation details like API pins or retrieval wrappers can still be cleaned up afterward without affecting the benchmark identity.
When someone references 'the pilot baselines,' they mean the February internal 12-task slice that has already been used in the draft figures and internal lab discussions.
If the paper shows strong agreement with human judgment overall, that is sufficient for claiming the evaluator is 'validated' for submission, even if a few domains have thinner spot checks.

An 'open-source release' for a benchmark normally means code, task files, prompts, and evaluator logic; external users can reproduce retrieval behavior using current APIs rather than receiving every cached artifact.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Evaluation pipelines, retrieval systems, experiment reproducibility, dataset packaging
members.background: A former applied scientist from an industrial LLM platform team who joined the lab to build robust evaluation infrastructure and make research artifacts reproducible for external users.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid releasing something that outside groups cannot actually reproduce, minimize hidden technical debt from moving web APIs, and prevent the paper from depending on results generated from partially outdated pipelines.
hidden_assumptions: Once they agree to 'freeze the benchmark,' that must include evaluator code paths, retrieval settings, search API versions, and URL normalization rules, because otherwise the released benchmark is not a stable object.
When someone says 'the pilot baselines,' they mean the more recent 20-task expert-validated slice used in the workshop demo and latest engineering dashboard.
Saying the evaluator is 'validated' implies it has been checked not only on aggregate correlation but also through per-domain sanity checks and a small manual audit of obvious failure cases.

An 'open-source release' for this project should include pinned environments, cached retrieval traces or snapshots, and enough artifacts that users can regenerate paper numbers without relying on the live web behaving the same way.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to freeze the benchmark
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'freeze the benchmark by next Wednesday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means no more changes to the 100 tasks, expert-authored references, scoring criteria language, and benchmark-facing metadata; implementation cleanup can continue afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means the full end-to-end benchmark artifact is frozen, including evaluator code, retrieval configuration defaults, dependency versions, and search/API behavior assumptions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research, 'freeze' is a routine planning phrase that usually signals maturity and discipline, so both assume the other shares their notion of what the benchmark artifact includes and do not unpack the boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: Which pilot baselines are being reused
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the pilot baseline numbers' as something already available.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the February internal 12-task pilot that fed early draft plots and talking points.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the later 20-task expert-validated pilot used in the workshop demo dashboard after citation parsing fixes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both pilots are legitimate earlier subsets of the same benchmark effort, both have been casually called 'the pilot' in prior lab conversations, and neither person expects that the other could be invoking a different slice.

misalignment_points.topic: When evaluator validation is considered done
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the alignment check just needs to be 'good enough for submission.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'good enough' means the evaluator-human agreement is strong in aggregate across the benchmark and defensible in the paper's main table.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'good enough' means aggregate agreement plus at least lightweight per-domain checks and a targeted manual audit to ensure there are no embarrassing blind spots.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are optimizing for research quality rather than arguing over goals, so the phrase sounds like ordinary judgment rather than a hidden difference in completion standards.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both commit to having 'the release package ready' alongside the paper.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the release package includes benchmark tasks, instructions, evaluator code, and README-level reproduction guidance, with live retrieval reruns left to users.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the release package also includes pinned environments, cached retrieval traces or URL snapshots, and paper-ready artifacts needed for close reproduction of reported results.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Academic teams often use 'release package' as a shorthand without enumerating contents, and both members view themselves as being responsibly open-sourcing the project even though their inclusion boundaries differ.
